o: Scan the string and return the letter whose second occurrence comes earliest. In "abccbaacz", 'c' recurs at index 3 before 'a' recurs at 5 or 'b' at 4, so the answer is 'c'. In "abcdd" only 'd' repeats. A single pass with a seen-set (or a 26-bit mask) solves it.
k: The answer is determined by the earliest second occurrence — one left-to-right scan with a 'seen' structure suffices.
A 26-bit integer bitmask replaces the hash set for O(1) constant-factor-faster membership tests.

a.i: Iterate characters; if a character was already seen, return it immediately; otherwise record it. The first repeat encountered in scan order is exactly the letter whose second occurrence is earliest.
s: For each c in s: if c in seen return c; add c to seen.
(Guaranteed to return inside the loop by the constraints.)
a.t: O(|s|) — single pass with O(1) set operations.

a.i: Keep an integer mask where bit (c − 'a') marks a seen letter. Testing and setting are single bitwise operations — a micro-optimization over the set that also demonstrates bit manipulation.
s: For each c: bit = 1 << (c − 'a'); if mask & bit return c; mask |= bit.
a.t: O(|s|) — single pass with bitwise operations.

w: Either approach is ideal; mention the bitmask to show bit fluency. Pitfall: confusing this with 'first non-repeating character' (opposite problem) or 'most frequent character' — here it is strictly the earliest second occurrence. Follow-up: return the letter with the earliest FIRST occurrence among letters appearing twice — requires recording first-seen indices and a second pass.
